coverage.method: Complete page text extracted from approved chunk PDFs in source order; PDF rendering separately recorded where layout or source uncertainty requires it.

findings.analytical_note: Robespierre tied democratic government to civic virtue and subordinated private interest to public good, while rejecting continuous direct action by the sovereign people. These arguments informed suspicion of moral deviation.

The committees’ motives and internal deliberations are poorly evidenced. Danton was tried on broad political allegations rather than corruption; a misleading report excluded defendants when their insistence on witnesses threatened conviction. Doyle interprets punishment as increasingly preventive and moralized, but explicitly retains uncertainty about motives.

Paris centralized conspiracy trials and removed procedural protections. June–July executions had a different social distribution from the Terror as a whole, suggesting that some died for identity or background as much as specific acts; preserve that qualified conclusion.
State control of the Commune brought wage repression and destruction of remaining protest institutions. July wage tables imposed cuts after earlier nominal increases, helping alienate workers.

The new cult asserted deity and immortality as supports for justice and virtue. Local practice ranged from reused reason-festival props to resumed mass; the coincidence with Whit Sunday is explicitly ambiguous. Robespierre’s prominence aroused ridicule and fear.

Personal conflict and overlapping police authority alarmed colleagues. Lack of consultation over the law and uncertainty about deputy immunity widened opposition; prominent public reputation did not equate to undisputed power.

reader_access_routes: Fouché and Tallien: coalition against Robespierre
findings.analytical_note: Victory weakened the emergency rationale for continued killing while mutual fear prevented agreement on ending it. Robespierre’s withdrawal and broad threats helped unite otherwise divided opponents.

A failed committee reconciliation preceded Robespierre’s denunciation of ill-specified conspirators. Control of the floor and a hostile majority produced arrest; his expectation of parliamentary support proved disastrous.

Only a minority of Guard companies rallied, and outlawry plus decisive Convention action dissolved resistance. Wage cuts, lack of planning, exhausted trust and official accusations together explain popular nonintervention.

reader_access_routes: Robespierre: assessment of power and intentions
findings.analytical_note: Doyle explicitly denies that Robespierre was a dictator or that reliable evidence proves he aimed to become one. Moral inflexibility and threats helped destroy him; survivors used the accusation to shift responsibility for acts they had shared.
The overthrow became rejection of a governing system. Rotating membership, renewed evidentiary requirements and redistribution of functions reduced concentrated power and executions.
Released prisoners’ resentment and organized street violence drove reaction. Competing claims about the factory explosion were political; the text considers it apparently accidental.

The Convention initially resisted wholesale prosecution of former leaders and signaled radical continuity, then restricted club networks and rewarded violent attacks by closing the Jacobins. Reaction was a contested process.

Some provincial courts continued after the Paris reversal. Replacement officials and released prisoners turned against former terrorists; Carrier’s execution individualized blame despite collective authorization and disputed attribution of atrocities.

Formal extension of controls gave way to abolition amid shortages and weakening support. Market-priced state procurement, weak tax receipts and expanded paper issues combined to collapse currency value; the source distinguishes these fiscal mechanisms from mere confidence.

Exceptional cold, frozen transport and mills, floods after thaw, poor harvest and army priorities caused a compound subsistence crisis. Fuel shortage defeated some substitutes; Paris’s relative ration protection did not describe provincial conditions.

Anti-Jacobin gangs policed songs, theaters and symbols. Babeuf’s constitutional call became a rallying point but initially prompted arrest, society closures and further repudiation of Year II martyrs.

Relaxation was selective. Ending public religious funding terminated the Revolution’s own established church and official Supreme Being cult, rather than simply restoring pre-revolutionary arrangements.

Freedom of worship retained bans on public signs, clerical dress and official support; congregations nonetheless rapidly found spaces and clergy. Formal legal toleration and uneven practical revival deserve separate routes.

Devastation and conscription prolonged insurgency. Religious concessions, amnesty, exemption and retained arms purchased apparent peace, but leaders’ motives differed and British expedition plans made some truces tactical.

Falling rations broke remaining confidence. The crowd disrupted the Convention without coherent organization or supportive deputies, then dispersed; repression and deportation of former committee leaders followed.
Disarmament and detention marked former activists as targets. Counter-terror included royalists but was mostly retaliatory and locally anarchic; its scale and danger varied sharply by region.

reader_access_routes: Prison massacres: Lyons, Aix, Tarascon, Marseilles
findings.analytical_note: Royalist networks and revenge gangs overlapped. Southeastern massacres often benefited from official connivance; Toulon’s pro-Jacobin response shows that anti-Jacobin reaction was not uniform.

Bread failure amid foreign victories prompted organized renewed action. Demands extended to independent Commune, permanent sections, food searches and prisoner releases; initial success induced deputies to support measures that were annulled after loyal forces recovered the hall.

Petition and dispersal surrendered initiative; siege and disarmament destroyed the surviving movement. The claim that Crest deputies planned the uprising is explicitly rejected; alleged deliberate delay by committees is reported as interpretation, not established fact.

Economic distress encouraged monarchist sentiment, but Provence’s declaration promised extensive restoration and excluded regicides from amnesty while leaving national lands unresolved. It undermined negotiated restoration and constitutional monarchism.

qualifications: The text itself dates Robespierre’s Convention speech to 26 July on p. 279 but calls it 27 July on p. 280; p. 280 then places Commune action on 28 July and entry into the Hôtel de Ville early 29 July. Retain source dates/sequence as supplied, with an internal consistency flag rather than an external correction.
Motives surrounding Danton’s fall, the Supreme Being festival’s relation to Whit Sunday, and some committee tactics in Prairial are explicitly uncertain or attributed interpretations.
